newsitem.title: INDIA: Sikh-Hindu alliance holds key in India's Punjab.
newsitem.headline: Sikh-Hindu alliance holds key in India's Punjab.

text.p: An alliance of pro-separatist Sikhs and rightwing Hindu nationalists is widely tipped to hold the key to the next government in India's sensitive border state of Punjab where local polls are scheduled for Friday.
Following are brief profiles of the major parties:
AKALI DAL (BADAL)

Headed by former Punjab chief minister Prakash Singh Badal, this main faction of the pro-separatist Sikh party is contesting 92 seats to the 117-member state assembly. It boycotted the last state assembly elections in 1992.
Badal's group has entered into a poll alliance with the rightwing Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) which is contesting the remaining 25 seats.
Badal has had frequent problems with New Delhi, particularly with the Congress party which has ruled India during most of the 50 years since independence.

The Akali Dal is committed to what is known as the "Anandpur Sahib Resolution" regarded as a manifesto for a separate homeland for India's Sikhs in Punjab. But the party has been careful not to emphasise the issue recently. to
BHARATIYA JANATA PARTY
India's main opposition party, the BJP is fighting the Punjab elections in tandem with the Akali Dal (Badal) but not without compromising its image as a hardline nationalist group.
The BJP-Akali Dal alliance is focusing in the Punjab polls on alleged corruption and political mismanagement during the state's Congress party government, which has ruled since 1992.
BJP leaders say they have gone into the alliance with Badal on specific issues which do not include their acceptance of his separatist doctrine.
CONGRESS PARTY
The Congress party, which won power in Punjab in 1992, is fighting the election on a campaign of peace and stability.
The party claims a major advantage in projecting Punjab Chief Minister Rajinder Kaur Bhattal as the state's first wowan leader.

The Congress, which is widely seen as eyeing political power in New Delhi by toppling a 13-party centre-left alliance it supports reluctantly, has scored a major political point by wooing the Communist Party of India to launch a joint campaign in Punjab.

Congress's major handicap in Punjab, as in several other states, is inner-party dissidence. Congress politicians say any setback for the party in Punjab will intensify divisions within the fractious group which only recently acquired a new president in Sitaram Kesri.
COMMUNIST PARTY OF INDIA

The smaller of the two main communist parties, the Communist Party of India (CPI) has evidently annoyed its left-wing allies by joining hands with the Congress party in Punjab. Members of the Left Front, led by the main Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPI-M), are key constitutents of Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's United Front alliance. The "straying" of the CPI from the group's policy of avoiding links with the Congress could have an impact on the national coalition, politicians say.
BAHUJAN SAMAJ PARTY

An influential group with credibildity among low caste Hindu and Sikh groups. The Bdahujan Samaj Party has deserted its national partner, the Congress party, to link up with another faction of the Akali Dal led by former police official turned separatist campaigner Simranjit Singh Mann, whose party boycotted the last state polls in Punjab in 1992.
